author: ribeye
dek: A software bug at JPMorgan Chase froze online banking and Zelle payments on Monday, and one Marysville household had to settle its debts the old-fashioned way: with actual paper money.
disclaimer: Parody: the Keller family of Marysville is fictional. The JPMorgan Chase outage and the Zelle payment delays are real, as reported by the Associated Press on Nov. 17, 2026.
headline: Marysville Family Discovers What Happens When Zelle Stops Zelling

ohio_story: MARYSVILLE, Ohio — Greg Keller knew something was wrong when the $40 he sends his babysitter every Friday refused to send on Monday. Keller, who works the early shift at the Honda plant, had already paid the neighbor kid for mowing the lawn, covered his daughter's fall soccer fees, and settled a fantasy football debt, all by phone, all without ever touching a dollar bill. On Monday, the phone had other ideas: the payment spun, the app apologized, and the bank's own message — "Some services aren't available. We're working on them. Please try back later" — offered no estimate of when later might arrive.

His wife, Amy, had her own crisis brewing at the kitchen table: the joint checking account would not load, the electric bill was due, and their 16-year-old daughter, Sophie, needed $25 for a school field trip by first period. "We found eleven dollars in the junk drawer, three in Greg's truck, and a five in a winter coat from last year," Amy said. "That is how we paid for babysitting in 2026. I am not proud of the math, but the math worked." Greg, meanwhile, drove to the Chase branch on Main Street, where the drive-up ATM was displaying its own version of the same apology, and came home with a new appreciation for the envelope of emergency cash his father has kept in a coffee can since 1987.

By Monday evening, with Chase saying the problem was a software bug and not a cyberattack, and Zelle insisting its own network was fine, the Kellers had a new family rule, written on the fridge in dry-erase marker next to the Marysville Monarchs schedule: keep forty dollars in cash in the house at all times. "I have spent ten years telling my kids that cash is dead," Greg said, staring at the five-dollar bill he had rescued from the winter coat. "Cash is not dead. Cash was just waiting in the coat closet for the internet to fail."
real_summary: Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said Monday that the problems were not the result of a cyberattack and that it was working to bring banking services back online by the end of the day.

JPMorgan Chase said it had "experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premises hardware system — it is not cyber-related," according to bank spokesman Joe Evangelisti, who added, "This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us." Some Chase customers received a message that read, "Some services aren't available. We're working on them. Please try back later." Banks including Bank of America and Citigroup were not having issues with their own banking services, though a U.S. Bank spokesman said clients sending or receiving Zelle payments with another financial institution might experience delays.

Zelle itself was not down: a spokesman for Early Warning Services, which owns Zelle, said the Zelle network was fully operational, and that "an issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers." The disruption came days after a run of technology failures across the U.S. economy: a global Microsoft 365 outage on Thursday, an FAA failure that grounded all U.S. flights on Friday, and an internal United Airlines system outage on Monday.
source_note: AP reporting, Nov. 17, 2026: JPMorgan Chase technical issue disrupts online banking and Zelle payments; software bug, not a cyberattack; Zelle network itself operational.
